Earlier this month, the ANC asked Mbeki to step down after a judge dismissed the corruption, fraud and racketeering case against Zuma, Mbeki’s political archrival. The judge declared the case invalid and accused Mbeki’s government of political interference.

“I depart this office knowing that many men and woman in South Africa have worked to achieve better lives for all,” Mbeki said.

Under his leadership, the country experienced the longest period of sustained economic growth in South Africa’s history and reached out to indigent people in an unprecedented way, Mbeki said. He also acknowledged that the country still faces economic, corruption and crime challenges in the future.

Mbeki gave his vote of confidence to the country’s next leader, though he did not name that person.

Gwede Mantashe, secretary-general of the African National Congress, announced Saturday that the party — with which Mbeki has been involved since his teens — had asked him to leave office before the end of his term. Mbeki agreed to do so, Mantashe said.

Mantashe said the ANC made the decision “for the citizens of South Africa, so there could be stability within the country” and so the ANC movement could remain “stable and unified.”

Political observers doubted that would happen because of Zuma’s popularity, particularly with the Communist Party and trade unions.

Zuma has denied the charges. He said the case was politically motivated and damaged his chances of becoming the ANC’s presidential nominee. If convicted of accepting bribes from a company that received a contract in a multibillion-dollar arms deal, he could have faced at least 15 years in prison.

Mbeki, 66, succeeded Nelson Mandela as South Africa’s president in June 1999. Critics alleged that he pushed for the corruption charges against Zuma.

Mbeki recently brokered a power-sharing deal between Zimbabwe’s political rivals, who signed the agreement on Monday in an effort to put aside a violent past and end the crisis that has paralyzed Zimbabwe since disputed national elections in March.

Under the agreement, longtime Zimbabwean leader Robert Mugabe remains president, while his perennial rival, Morgan Tsvangirai, has become prime minister and coordinator of government affairs.

Mbeki publicly announced in a televised speech on Sunday that he would step down. Kgalema Motlanthe, deputy president of the African National Congress, has been chosen to replace him and is scheduled to be sworn in as South Africa’s president on Thursday.

After Mbeki said he would resign, several members of his Cabinet indicated they might also leave their posts. However, according to government sources, Mbeki encouraged them to remain in office.

A government statement said the resignations — including those of Finance Minister Trevor Manuel and Defense Minister Mosiuoa Lekota — will become effective Thursday, the same day Mbeki formally departs.

“All the ministers have expressed their availability to assist the incoming administration in the hand-over process and any other assistance that might be sought from them,” the statement said.

An aide to the finance minister told CNN that Manuel would be prepared to take a position in the new government if asked. The government also said three deputy ministers had handed in resignations.

A spokesperson for the ruling African National Congress confirmed that the party had selected Motlanthe to succeed Mbeki. Motlanthe is expected to serve until elections scheduled for the spring of the following year, which ANC President Jacob Zuma is broadly expected to win.

Earlier in the month, the ANC called on Mbeki to resign after a judge dismissed corruption, fraud and racketeering charges against Zuma, Mbeki’s major political rival. The judge ruled the case invalid and accused Mbeki’s administration of political meddling.

Mbeki, who had led South Africa for almost a decade, used his televised resignation speech on Sunday to highlight parts of his record.

“I depart this office knowing that many men and woman in South Africa have worked to achieve better lives for all,” Mbeki said.

He said that during his presidency South Africa experienced the longest stretch of continuous economic expansion in its history and made unprecedented efforts to assist poor citizens.

Mbeki also acknowledged that the nation would continue to face serious problems, including economic difficulties, corruption and crime. Without identifying his successor by name, he expressed confidence in South Africa’s next leader.

Gwede Mantashe, the ANC’s secretary-general, said Saturday that the party — with which Mbeki had been associated since his teenage years — had asked him to step down before the end of his term. Mbeki agreed, Mantashe said.

According to Mantashe, the ANC made the decision “for the citizens of South Africa, so there could be stability within the country” and to ensure that the ANC movement stayed “stable and unified.”

The case against Zuma, who took over from Mbeki as ANC president the previous year, was first dismissed in September 2006, but South Africa’s National Prosecuting Authority later brought the charges again. Judge Chris Nicholson did not determine whether Zuma was guilty or innocent, meaning prosecutors could still charge him again.

Political analysts, however, questioned whether that would happen because Zuma remained popular, especially among trade unions and the Communist Party.

Zuma has rejected the accusations. He has argued that the case was driven by politics and damaged his prospects of becoming the ANC’s presidential candidate.

If found guilty of taking bribes from a company that received a contract in a multibillion-dollar arms agreement, Zuma could have faced at least 15 years in prison. He was also accused of maintaining a corrupt relationship with his former financial adviser, Schabir Shaik. Shaik is serving a 15-year prison sentence for seeking bribes on Zuma’s behalf and using Zuma’s political influence to advance his own business interests.

Mbeki, 66, became South Africa’s president in June 1999, succeeding Nelson Mandela. His critics claimed he had pressed for the corruption case against Zuma to be pursued.

More recently, Mbeki mediated a power-sharing agreement between rival political factions in Zimbabwe. The deal, signed on Monday, was intended to move beyond political violence and resolve the crisis that had gripped Zimbabwe since disputed national elections in March.

Under the agreement, longtime Zimbabwean leader Robert Mugabe remained president, while his longtime opponent Morgan Tsvangirai became prime minister and took on responsibility for coordinating government affairs.

The ruling did not acquit Zuma, but its political implications were explosive.

The ANC leadership interpreted the judgment as evidence that state institutions had been used in internal party battles. Mbeki denied interfering in the prosecution and said he was resigning to preserve the unity of the party and the country.

His departure triggered a wave of Cabinet resignations. Mbeki, who has led Africa’s largest economy since 1999, told the nation that he had accepted the ANC’s decision to “recall” him from office, a move that followed a bruising internal party battle with ANC president Jacob Zuma and a court ruling that raised questions about political interference in Zuma’s corruption prosecution.

“I have been a loyal member of the African National Congress for 52 years,” Mbeki said in a calm, carefully worded address broadcast nationally. “I therefore respect its decisions and will do so even in this instance.” He said he would formally tender his resignation to Parliament, and emphasized that the transfer of authority would proceed in accordance with the Constitution.

Mbeki rejected allegations that he or his government had improperly influenced prosecutors in cases involving Zuma, saying he had never interfered with the National Prosecuting Authority. “We have never done this and never compromised the right of the National Prosecuting Authority to decide whom it should prosecute,” he said.

The announcement capped months of political turmoil inside the ANC, which has governed South Africa since Nelson Mandela led it to victory in the country’s first democratic elections in 1994. The party’s National Executive Committee decided over the weekend to remove Mbeki before the end of his second term, which was due to expire after national elections in 2009.

ANC leaders said the decision was necessary to restore political stability after a Sept. 12 ruling by High Court Judge Chris Nicholson, who dismissed corruption charges against Zuma on procedural grounds and suggested there may have been political meddling in the case. Though the government and prosecutors disputed that implication, the ruling emboldened Zuma’s supporters, who have long claimed that the charges were part of a campaign to block him from becoming president.

Zuma, a former deputy president whom Mbeki dismissed in 2005 after Zuma’s financial adviser was convicted of corruption, has faced a series of legal and political battles. He was acquitted of rape in 2006, but corruption allegations linked to South Africa’s multibillion-dollar arms procurement program continued to shadow his political rise. His supporters portray him as the victim of an establishment hostile to his populist appeal; critics say the unresolved allegations raise serious concerns about governance and the rule of law.

With Mbeki stepping down, the ANC moved quickly to reassure markets and foreign governments that the transition would be orderly. Motlanthe, a former trade unionist and ANC secretary-general who was appointed to the Cabinet earlier this year, emerged as the party’s preferred candidate to serve as interim president until elections next year. Parliament is expected to elect him in the coming days.

Motlanthe is widely viewed as a steady, pragmatic figure capable of bridging the party’s rival factions. His expected elevation is also seen as a way to avoid placing Zuma directly in the presidency before the 2009 elections, while keeping Zuma on track as the ANC’s likely presidential candidate.

The transition comes at a sensitive moment for South Africa’s regional diplomacy. Just days before his recall, Mbeki helped broker a power-sharing agreement in neighboring Zimbabwe between President Robert Mugabe and opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai after months of violence and political deadlock following disputed elections. The deal, signed in Harare on Sept. 15, created a framework for Mugabe to remain president while Tsvangirai would become prime minister, though major questions remain over control of key ministries and the security services.

Mbeki’s Zimbabwe mediation has been both praised and criticized. Supporters say his quiet diplomacy was instrumental in bringing Mugabe and Tsvangirai to the negotiating table. Detractors argue that he was too lenient toward Mugabe and failed to speak forcefully against state-backed intimidation and economic mismanagement that have devastated Zimbabwe.

At home, Mbeki leaves behind a mixed legacy. He presided over years of economic growth and the expansion of a black middle class, but his administration was criticized for high unemployment, widening inequality, violent crime and its controversial response to the HIV/AIDS epidemic. His aloof governing style also alienated many within the ANC, while Zuma built a broad coalition among trade unions, communists, youth activists and grassroots party members.

Mbeki’s defeat inside the ANC began in earnest in December 2007, when Zuma beat him for the party presidency at a bitter conference in Polokwane. Although Mbeki remained national president, the loss stripped him of control over the party machinery and set up months of uneasy cohabitation between the government and the ANC leadership.

The party’s decision to remove him early underscores the depth of the rift. Several Cabinet ministers loyal to Mbeki are expected to consider their positions, raising the possibility of further resignations and a reshuffle under Motlanthe.

Still, ANC officials insisted the country’s institutions remain stable. South Africa’s Constitution provides that when a president resigns, the National Assembly elects a new president from among its members. Once elected, the new president must be sworn in and appoint a Cabinet.

For now, the party that led South Africa out of apartheid is attempting to manage its first forced presidential exit without alarming citizens, investors or regional partners. Mbeki, in his farewell address, appealed for unity and restraint.

“I am convinced that the incoming administration will continue to do everything possible to ensure that our country remains on course,” he said.

But the political center of gravity has unmistakably shifted. Mbeki, once one of Africa’s most influential leaders, is leaving office under pressure from his own movement. Zuma, despite continuing legal controversy, stands closer than ever to the presidency. And Motlanthe is poised to become the caretaker leader of a country entering an uncertain new era.
